summary: Orbit Care is a private self-check companion for astronauts on long-duration missions, built around isolation and distance from Earth. A sensor ring tracks heart rate, heart-rate variability , skin temperature and sleep against each astronaut's own baseline. When those readings drift, Orbit Care raises a "change in your rhythm" alert and guides a 2-minute self-check: symptoms, a reaction-time fatigue test and a blood pressure reading, ending in one clear next step. Daily emotional check-ins use four feeling planets; an on-device engine compares words with body data, explains what it notices, and forecasts tomorrow. A clickable body map links each reading to a NASA Human Research Program risk and says when to call ground. Common Room, Tether (light-delay messaging home) and a locked private space, Haven, support connection and the things crews rarely say aloud, including sexual and pelvic health.
details:
What it does

On a Mars transit there is no doctor down the hall and every message to Earth takes minutes. Astronauts have to notice changes in themselves. Orbit Care turns that into a 30-second habit, and a 2-minute check when the body asks for one.

1. Home: four grainy feeling planets (wound up, lit up, weighed down, settled), labelled by energy and pleasantness. Tapping one sends it around its orbit into the check-in.

2. Rhythm alert and self-check: when overnight data drifts from personal baseline (for example HRV -27%, resting heart rate +10, third night under 6 h), an amber alert appears. It opens a 2-minute self-check: symptoms and sleep, a 5-round reaction test modelled on the psychomotor vigilance test, ring heart rate and cuff blood pressure. The result is one next step: carry on, protect the next 24 hours, or send just these results to the crew medical officer.

3. Check-in: the closest word, context tags (with "add your own" and a "just in my mind" option) and one optional journal line.

4. Companion: an on-device reading engine compares the chosen feeling with what heart rate and sleep alone suggest, lists what it notices with evidence, suggests one action, forecasts tomorrow ("sleep 7 h tonight and the chance of a tense or low day drops from 73% to 56%"), and offers a consent-based summary for the flight surgeon only when a pattern warrants it.

5. Body: a particle figure you scrub with a finger. Each region (head, chest, arms & hands, stomach, pelvis, hips & legs) shows its readings, color-coded status, the matching NASA HRP risk, what to do today and when to call ground. Manual readings come with measuring steps and input validation.

6. History: one point per day by energy, patterns found automatically, and sleep, HRV and resting-heart-rate trends against baseline.

7. Common Room: crew posts, "I'm in" for plans, a quiet "with you", and opt-in crew weather that shares your planet, never your words.

8. Tether: messages home travel along an arc with a live light-delay countdown; each contact shows their Earth local time.

9. Haven: a press-and-hold private room with a privacy ledger, a pressure valve (write it, then keep it or let it dissolve unsaved) and an intimacy & release check-in in clinical language. Never synced; locks on idle, backgrounding, or when a crewmate approaches.

10. Profile: the Orbit Ring hardware, personal baseline, radiation dose, reminders and exactly what ground may see.

How it works

Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no backend and no network calls, so it would run on an isolated spacecraft network. Every metric is compared with the astronaut's own rolling baseline. The reading engine is transparent and rule-based; each insight shows its evidence. Data stays on the device.

Benefits

Earlier, self-directed detection of fatigue, stress and isolation effects; less dependence on real-time ground contact; more honest reporting because privacy is built in rather than promised.

What we hope to achieve

Pair it with a real ring SDK, validate thresholds with flight surgeons, and test it in an analog habitat (HERA or CHAPEA style) to see whether body-mind agreement improves over a mission.

Tools

HTML, CSS, vanilla JavaScript, Canvas 2D, SVG, localStorage; designed in Figma; hosted on GitHub Pages; font Jost (Google Fonts, SIL Open Font License).

Source code: https://github.com/JzC33/24-7_NASA_Orbit-Care
